Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
237 AM EDT Sun Aug 16 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 237 AM EDT Sunday...

Beneficial rainfall remains on track for tonight. Slightly
greater potential for a thunderstorm Monday afternoon/evening.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 237 AM EDT Sunday...

1. Pleasant conditions through the daylight hours today.
Widespread showers with beneficial rainfall tonight will be followed 
by scattered showers and localized thunderstorms Monday. 

2. A narrow ridge of high pressure and seasonable warmth for 
Tuesday will give way to another weak frontal system that brings 
shower and thunderstorm chances Wednesday. 

3. Climatological conditions persist through the second half of 
the week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 237 AM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A mid-level trough and the associated warm air advection 
ahead of this feature should produce enough ascent for widespread 
showers this evening, generally starting in New York and spreading 
north and east with time. A band of heavier rainfall rates still 
appears possible overnight, and model guidance that shows this 
feature continues to favor northern and northeastern Vermont 
primarily with greater likelihood of rainfall amounts of around 0.5" 
to 1" and locally greater than 1". Meanwhile a quarter inch or less, 
with many areas seeing only 0.1" or so, is expected for most areas 
through the nighttime hours. While we continue to expect a surge of 
PWAT and warm cloud depth values that typically are associated with 
our heavy rainfall events, instability looks scant (Most Unstable 
CAPE < 300 J/kg) and rain showers fast moving such that downpours 
will be very brief in nature. The upper level pattern doesn't appear 
conducive to a heavy rain event, as there will be a split in the 
flow with two competing areas of forcing; one passing to our north, 
which will primarily affect our region, and another wave well to our 
south, where the primary deep moisture and convective threat will 
lie.

Perhaps more interesting will be the showers that develop during the 
day tomorrow, which may be capable of producing lightning as the 
environment becomes marginally conducive for thunderstorms. Overall 
the threat for any strong thunderstorms is very low and severe 
weather is not expected. The greatest risk area seems to be from 
eastern Essex County, New York and into the southern Champlain 
Valley, although broadly a 20-25% chance of thunder during the 
afternoon exists for the Adirondacks and much Vermont. Dew points 
increasing into the mid and upper 60s and limited sunshine will aid 
in some modest surface-based instability with showers developing 
with relatively shallow cloud bases. PWAT remains elevated (roughly 
1.4 to 1.6 inches) with ensemble mean surface based instability 
climbing into the 750-1250 J/kg range during peak heating in 
northeastern New York, where a subtle convergence line should set up 
to help showers blossom and organize. Effective shear looks 
relatively low (25 or so knots), limiting the potential for any 
stronger storms, although terrain driven convergence in the western 
Champlain Valley could help strengthen cells that move through. The 
showers will gradually move south and eastward, as the 
boundary/trough exits Vermont sometime in the evening. Rainfall will 
be highly variable, with some localized areas likely seeing around 
an inch of new rainfall but most areas seeing only an additional few 
hundreths to a quarter inch.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The next noteworthy period of weather will be on 
Wednesday when there is broad consensus that a fairly weak cold 
front will pass through the Northeast. Timing of the front is 
generally appears to be during the day with primarily chances for 
showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. 
The details and potential for multiple boundaries to move through 
the region will need to be hashed out in the coming days. That being 
said, some deterministic model guidance suggests the pre-frontal 
environment will be devoid of instability and moisture such that 
little in the way of thunderstorm, let alone shower, activity will 
occur. Per ensemble guidance, the risk of thunderstorms, along with 
rain chances, is perhaps a bit higher in the St. Lawrence Valley 
than areas to the east, but we'll watch trends in the coming days.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Lingering showers will move out through the day 
Thursday, as broad cyclonic flow slowly migrates eastward. After
the system moves off, a period of drier weather looks to return
for the latter half of the week. Daytime temperatures will 
fluctuate near climatological normals in the mid 70s, with 
overnight lows falling into the low 60s. There is potential for 
another system to sweep through next weekend bringing some 
sustained showers. We'll continue to monitor as the models lock 
in.


&&

.AVIATION /06Z SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 06Z Monday...Fog formation will be slightly less widespread
than last night, but we continue to anticipate development in the
favored areas. Dew point depression has reached zero at SLK, with
MPV and EFK not far behind. The fog will burn off in the morning,
leaving us with VFR conditions throughout the day tomorrow before
rain falls tomorrow night.

Outlook...

Monday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Slight chance SHRA.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Thursday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
